questions.question: What is the difference between function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions?
questions.title: JavaScript function forms
questions.direct_answer: A function declaration creates a hoisted function binding, while a function expression creates a function value when its expression is evaluated. An arrow function is a compact function expression with lexical this and no own arguments, prototype, or constructor capability, so it is not a drop-in replacement for every regular function.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether syntax forms are connected to binding and invocation semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an arrow as a method that expects receiver-based this.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Function declarations can be called before their declaration is evaluated.
Function expressions become available when their assignment runs.
Arrow functions capture this from the surrounding scope.
Arrow functions have no own arguments or prototype and cannot be constructors.
Choose a form from semantics and readability, not line count alone.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- A function declaration defines a named function binding for its scope and is initialized during scope creation, so code in that scope can call it before the declaration appears in source order.

- A function expression produces a function value when evaluation reaches the expression. For example, assigning one to a `const` means the binding follows `const` temporal-dead-zone rules. Named function expressions can still provide a useful internal name for recursion and stack traces.

- An arrow function is a function expression with lexical `this`, `arguments`, `super`, and `new.target`. It cannot be called with `new` and has no own `prototype`. This makes arrows a natural fit for short callbacks that should keep the surrounding `this`.

- A regular method is usually better when `this` should be chosen by the receiver at call time, and a declaration is clear for a reusable top-level operation. The forms can execute similar bodies, but their initialization and invocation semantics determine the correct choice.

sections.title: Syntax carries initialization and call semantics
sections.content: The meaningful differences appear before the body runs: when the binding exists, whether a caller supplies this, and whether construction or an arguments object is supported.

sections.title: Name and binding are separate concerns
sections.content:
A declaration places its name in the surrounding scope. An anonymous expression can be inferred from its assignment name, while a named expression also creates a name visible inside its own body. That internal name helps recursive calls remain stable even if the outer variable changes.

Arrow functions should not be used as object methods when the method needs the object as dynamic `this`. `call`, `apply`, and `bind` cannot replace an arrow's lexical this value.

sections.title: Function form semantics
sections.content:
| Form | Available before line? | Own dynamic `this`? | Construct with `new`? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Declaration | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Function expression | After evaluation | Yes | Usually yes |
| Arrow function | After evaluation | No | No |

questions.question: How does lexical scope work in JavaScript?
questions.title: Lexical scope and the scope chain
questions.direct_answer: JavaScript uses lexical scope: a name is resolved from where a function or block is written. The engine checks the current environment, then each enclosing environment until it finds the binding or reaches the global/module boundary. Calling a function from a different location does not change that scope chain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether scope is tied to definition location and environment lookup.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the caller's local variables become visible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separating lexical scope from prototype property lookup.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Scope follows source nesting, not the caller's location.
Name lookup begins in the current lexical environment.
An inner binding can shadow an outer binding with the same name.
Blocks scope let, const, and class declarations; var is function-scoped.
Assigning an undeclared name is an error in strict mode and should never be used.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- Lexical scope means the visible names of a function are determined by where that function is defined in the source. At runtime, name lookup begins in the current environment and moves outward through enclosing environments.

- For example, a function defined inside `createGreeting` can read that call's `prefix` even when the returned function is later invoked from another file or callback. The call site does not supply a new lexical parent.

- A nested declaration with the same name shadows the outer binding inside its scope. `let`, `const`, and class declarations are block-scoped, while `var` belongs to the nearest function or global scope. Parameters are bindings in the function's environment as well.

- This model makes dependencies predictable and enables closures. Its boundary is accidental shadowing or global state: reusing a broad name can hide the value a reader expects, and undeclared assignments can create legacy global properties outside strict mode. I keep scopes narrow, use modules, and pass true dependencies explicitly.

sections.title: Name lookup walks outward, never sideways
sections.content: A scope can see its own bindings and those of lexical ancestors. It cannot directly see sibling or child scopes, and a caller's local variables do not become visible to the called function.

sections.title: Environment records hold different binding kinds
sections.content:
Function calls create environments for parameters and local declarations. Blocks may create additional lexical environments. Modules have their own environment whose imports are live read-only bindings to exports from other modules.

Scope is not the same as object property lookup. Resolving `user.name` first resolves the variable `user` lexically, then the property access algorithm finds `name` on the object or its prototype chain.

sections.title: Resolving a name
sections.content:
current block environment
  ↓ not found
current function environment
  ↓ not found
enclosing function/module environment
  ↓ not found
ReferenceError

questions.question: How does this differ in arrow functions and regular functions?
questions.title: this in arrow and regular functions
questions.direct_answer: A regular function's this is selected by how the function is called: as a method, with new, through call/apply/bind, or as a plain function. An arrow function has no own this and reads the this value of its surrounding lexical scope, so rebinding methods cannot change it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether this is explained from invocation form rather than location alone.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an arrow method expecting the containing object as this.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connecting bind to new function identity and listener cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Regular-function this is determined at the call site.
obj.method() normally sets this to obj.
Arrow functions capture this from the surrounding lexical scope.
call, apply, and bind cannot replace an arrow's captured this.
Use a regular method when the receiver should supply this.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `this` in a regular function is not determined where the function is written. It depends on the invocation form. Calling `user.show()` sets `this` to `user`; extracting the same function and calling it plainly loses that receiver, and strict-mode `this` is then `undefined`.

- Arrow functions do not create their own `this`. They close over the surrounding value. For example, an arrow callback inside a regular method can read `this.items` from that method without storing `const self = this`.

- That same feature makes an arrow a poor object method when it needs the object receiver. Defining `show: () => this.name` captures the outer scope; it does not make `this` the object containing the property.

- `call`, `apply`, and `bind` choose `this` for regular functions, while `bind` cannot replace an arrow's lexical value. Class methods are regular functions and class bodies are strict. I use regular methods for receiver-based behaviour and arrows for callbacks that intentionally inherit surrounding context.

sections.title: this is an invocation input for regular functions
sections.content: Method syntax stores an ordinary function in a property. The receiver comes from the call expression, which is why separating the function from the object changes its this value.

sections.title: Binding a method creates another function
sections.content:
`user.show.bind(user)` returns a new function whose this is fixed. That new identity matters for event listener cleanup. `call` invokes immediately with a chosen this and arguments; `apply` does the same with an array-like argument list.

Constructor calls create a new object and bind it as this before the regular function body runs. Arrows cannot participate because they have no `[[Construct]]` capability.

sections.title: How this is selected
sections.content:
| Call form | Regular function `this` | Arrow function `this` |
|---|---|---|
| `obj.fn()` | `obj` | surrounding lexical value |
| `fn()` in strict mode | `undefined` | surrounding lexical value |
| `fn.call(x)` | `x` | surrounding lexical value |
| `new Fn()` | new instance | not allowed |
